title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TELL A MAN TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY Instead of Pretending Bodies Don’t Matter?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TELL A MAN TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY Instead of Pretending Bodies Don’t Matter?
Proverbs 5:18–19 says something about marriage, desire, and the human body that many Christians are almost embarrassed to admit is actually in the Bible.
There are verses Christians whisper about.
Verses we read quickly when the children are in the room.
Verses that somehow never make it onto the coffee mug.
And then there is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read it slowly, because the Bible is far less embarrassed about God’s design for married love than many of us have become.
The Hebrew says:
יְהִֽי־מְקוֹרְךָ֥ בָר֑וּךְ וּ֝שְׂמַ֗ח מֵאֵ֥שֶׁת נְעוּרֶֽךָ׃
אַיֶּ֥לֶת אֲהָבִ֗ים וְֽיַעֲלַת־חֵ֥ן דַּ֭דֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּ֣ךָ בְכָל־עֵ֑ת בְּ֝אַהֲבָתָ֗הּ תִּשְׁגֶּ֥ה תָמִֽיד׃

“Let your fountain be blessed: Find joy in the wife of your youth—a loving doe, a graceful mountain goat. Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be infatuated with love of her always.” Proverbs 5:18–19, Revised JPS.
Yes.
The Hebrew really says that.
The word is דַּדֶּיהָ — daddeha — “her breasts.”
The text does not hide the body behind a cloud of religious euphemisms.
And perhaps that makes some of us uncomfortable because somewhere along the way, many Christians learned an idea that did not actually come from the Bible:
That holiness means pretending physical attraction does not matter.
But Proverbs does something radically different.
It does not tell the husband to become blind to his wife’s body.
It tells him where his eyes, affection, desire, delight, and covenant loyalty belong.
With her.
That changes everything.
Because Proverbs 5 is not pornography dressed up as Scripture.
It is almost the exact opposite.

The chapter begins with a father warning his son about sexual temptation. The seductive alternative initially appears sweet, but the path ends in devastation. Then comes the breathtaking counter-command: do not merely spend your entire life saying “no” to forbidden desire.
Learn the holy place where desire can say “yes.”
“Drink water from your own cistern,” Proverbs says.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Remain captivated by her love.
And then, immediately after these words, verse 20 asks why the son should become captivated by a forbidden woman instead. Verse 21 reminds him that his ways are before the eyes of the LORD.
That context matters enormously.
God is not teaching men to objectify women.
He is teaching a husband to direct sexual desire toward covenant faithfulness rather than adultery.
There is a difference between delighting in your wife and reducing your wife to a body.
A massive difference.
One says, “Your body exists for my consumption.”
The other says, “You are my beloved covenant companion, and I refuse to pretend that the physical dimension of our marriage is somehow beneath God.”
Biblical desire is never permission for selfishness, coercion, humiliation, comparison, entitlement, or abuse.
The woman being celebrated in Proverbs 5 is not a product.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
There is history there.
Covenant.
Years.
Memories.
Ordinary mornings.
Private laughter.
Arguments survived.
Tears witnessed.
Children perhaps raised.
Bodies that change.
Hair that changes.
Faces that change.
Strength that changes.
Seasons that change.
And Scripture still says:
Rejoice in her.
Maybe somebody needs to hear that.
Because we live in a culture trained to discard bodies when they change.
The world says youth is desirable.
God teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world says compare.
Covenant says cherish.
The world says scroll until somebody more attractive appears.
Wisdom says come home.
And suddenly Proverbs 5 becomes painfully contemporary.
The forbidden woman may not be standing at somebody’s doorway anymore.
She can appear through a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning.
She can be an old flame rediscovered online.
A secret conversation.
A private browser.
A fantasy carefully hidden from a spouse.
A relationship at work that supposedly “isn’t anything.”
One more message.
One more picture.
One more compromise.
One more secret.
Until a man wakes up and realizes that he has been feeding his appetite everywhere except the covenant where God called him to cultivate love.
That is why this passage is not merely about breasts.
It is about direction.
Where is your desire going?
Where is your attention going?
Where is your imagination going?
Where is the tenderness going that your spouse once received?
Where are your eyes going when nobody else can see them?
Because God can.
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
That comes immediately after this teaching.
Not because God despises desire.
Because He sees what desire can become when it escapes wisdom.
And here is where the Gospel has to enter this conversation.
Because some people reading this already feel condemned.
Maybe pornography has been part of your secret life.
Maybe emotional infidelity crossed lines you promised yourself you would never cross.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you have spent years comparing your spouse to edited bodies on a screen.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe physical intimacy became transactional.
Maybe resentment entered the bedroom years ago and never left.
Maybe you are the spouse who was betrayed.
Maybe these verses hurt because your body has been criticized instead of cherished.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time you felt wanted.
Maybe you have carried shame about your body since childhood.
Maybe religious environments taught you that your body itself was dirty.
Maybe someone used “submission” or “marital duty” as religious language to pressure you, and now even biblical passages about intimacy make your body tense.
Hear this carefully.
Proverbs 5 does not give anyone permission to abuse you.
Marriage does not transform selfishness into holiness.
Sexual coercion does not become righteous because somebody attaches a Bible verse to it.
Biblical marital intimacy belongs within covenant love, faithfulness, mutual care, honor, and self-giving.

The New Testament makes that mutuality strikingly clear. In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul speaks to both husband and wife about marital affection and mutual responsibility. Neither spouse is presented as a disposable object existing merely for the gratification of the other.
And Christ gives us an even deeper pattern for love.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is Ephesians 5:25.
Gave Himself.
That is the shape of Christian love.
Not “How much can I take?”
“How can I give?”
Not domination.
Sacrifice.
Not consumption.
Covenant.
Not using another body.
Cherishing another person.
And suddenly Proverbs 5:19 and Ephesians 5:25 belong in the same marriage.
Desire and sacrifice.
Delight and devotion.
Attraction and covenant.
Body and soul.
This is something Christians desperately need to recover.
The body is not the enemy of spirituality.
God created human beings embodied.
Before sin entered the story, Genesis says the man and woman were naked and unashamed.
Christianity does not ultimately teach escape from embodiment. The Christian hope includes resurrection.
And at the center of Christianity stands one of the most astonishing claims imaginable:
“The Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ did not save humanity by pretending physical existence was beneath Him.
He entered it.
Of course, none of that means every bodily appetite is automatically holy.
Hunger can become gluttony.
Anger can become violence.
Sexual desire can become lust, exploitation, adultery, pornography, selfishness, or idolatry.
The answer is not to declare the body evil.
The answer is redemption.
Desire needs discipleship.
And that is exactly what Proverbs 5 is doing.
It takes sexual desire by the shoulders, turns it away from betrayal, and points it home.
To your covenant.
To your spouse.
To faithfulness.
To gratitude.
To delight without betrayal.
There is another uncomfortable truth here.
Some married Christians have become experts at resisting adultery while forgetting to cultivate affection.
They never physically cheated.
But somewhere along the way they stopped seeing each other.
Stopped flirting.
Stopped touching without an agenda.
Stopped complimenting.
Stopped listening.
Stopped laughing.
Stopped dating.
Stopped protecting time together.
Stopped saying, “You are beautiful to me.”
Then they wonder why the marriage feels like two exhausted roommates managing bills, children, laundry, and calendars.
Proverbs does not merely say:
Do not commit adultery.
It says:
Rejoice.
That Hebrew command is וּשְׂמַח — u-semach — “and rejoice,” “be glad,” “take joy.”
That is active language.
Marital faithfulness is more than refusing to leave.
It is learning, again and again, how to come home.
And verse 19 becomes even more startling.
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד

The translations capture the intensity differently: be captivated, intoxicated, infatuated with her love continually. The Hebrew imagery is strong enough that several major translations preserve that sense of being deeply overcome or exhilarated by marital love.
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
It takes language of overwhelming desire and places it inside covenant.
Not outside marriage.
Inside it.
God is not saying attraction is irrelevant.
He is saying attraction is not your god.
It must learn covenant.
And this matters when bodies change.
Because they will.
Pregnancy changes bodies.
Childbirth changes bodies.
Illness changes bodies.
Medication changes bodies.
Stress changes bodies.
Age changes bodies.
Gravity is undefeated.
The twenty-five-year-old body will not remain twenty-five.
Neither will yours.
And if your definition of marital delight survives only while another human being looks young, then you have confused covenant love with consumer preference.
Biblical marital love can acknowledge beauty without worshiping youth.
It can celebrate physical attraction without making physical perfection the admission price for affection.
A Christian husband should never weaponize Proverbs 5:19 against a wife whose body has changed.
Think about the cruelty of that.
The woman who carried your children should not have to compete with digitally altered strangers for the eyes of the man who promised to cherish her.
The husband aging beside his wife should not have to believe his worth disappears when his hair thins, his strength changes, or his body bears the evidence of years.
Marriage says:
I know what time has done to you.
Time has touched me too.
Come here.
I still choose you.
That may be one of the most beautiful things an aging couple can say without speaking.
And maybe that is why this passage reaches deeper than sexuality.
It exposes our entire theology of faithfulness.
God does not call us to a disposable love.
And neither does the Gospel.
Jesus did not look at ruined sinners and say, “Come back when you are more desirable.”
He came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with the despised.
He called the guilty to repentance.
He carried a cross.
He shed His blood.
He rose from the grave.
And He still calls sinners home.

Be careful here: Christ’s redeeming love for His people is not identical to marital erotic desire. Scripture uses marriage imagery for Christ and the church in its own theological way, and we should not collapse those categories.
But Christian marriage can still point beyond itself.
Forgiveness points beyond itself.
Faithfulness points beyond itself.
Sacrificial love points beyond itself.
Covenant points beyond itself.
And for the person reading this who has already failed sexually, the final word of Christianity is not:
Scandal.
It is not:
Ruined.
It is not:
Unclean forever.
It is not:
Too late.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Repentance does not mean pretending the sin never happened.
Grace does not mean calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence.
But the blood of Christ is sufficient for the genuinely repentant sinner.
There is forgiveness for the adulterer.
There is forgiveness for the pornography addict.
There is forgiveness for the person who cultivated secret fantasies.
There is forgiveness for the husband who neglected his wife.
There is forgiveness for the wife who hardened herself in bitterness.
There is forgiveness for sexual sin you would rather die than let anyone discover.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
Jesus does not invite us to rename darkness.
He calls us out of it.
Repent.
Confess.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where necessary.
If another person has been harmed, do not use “God forgave me” as a weapon to silence their pain or escape accountability.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace kneels.
Grace repents.
Grace makes restitution where possible.
Grace learns new patterns.
Grace closes secret doors.
Grace deletes numbers.
Grace installs boundaries.
Grace asks for help.
Grace stops blaming the spouse for personal sin.
Grace says, “Jesus, I cannot keep living two lives.”
And grace gets back up after failure and keeps walking toward Christ.
Maybe you need to whisper that right now.
Jesus, forgive me.
Maybe nobody around you knows what that sentence means.
He does.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing words into a comment section saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe you are fighting hard to stay faithful while your marriage is going through an incredibly dry season.
Maybe betrayal has left you wondering whether your heart will ever feel safe again.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity publicly while privately collapsing.
And if you cannot find many words at all, simply write:
Let believers pray for believers.
Let wounded people discover they are not the only wounded people in the room.
Let testimonies meet confession.
Let grace interrupt shame.
And husbands, hear Proverbs again.
Your wife is not invisible.
Your wife is not a household appliance.
She is not merely “the mother of the children.”
She is not supposed to spend her marriage wondering why you can notice every beautiful woman on a screen but no longer notice her.
Look at her.
Not merely at her body.
At her.
Remember the woman you prayed for.
Remember the conversations that lasted until ridiculous hours.
Remember the first time you realized you loved her.
Remember the years she has walked beside you.
Remember what the two of you survived.
And yes—within the tenderness, privacy, mutuality, and holiness of your marriage—delight in her physically too.
The Bible is not embarrassed to say it.
Neither should we be.
Wives, this is not a command to achieve some impossible beauty standard so that your husband will remain faithful.
His faithfulness is his responsibility before God.
You do not have to defeat aging to deserve covenant faithfulness.
And husbands, your wife is not responsible for becoming every image your undisciplined imagination has consumed.
Perhaps the deeper repentance for some men is not asking their wives to become more visually stimulating.
Perhaps it is retraining eyes that have been overstimulated by a world designed to monetize lust.
Come home.
Come home with your body.
Come home with your eyes.
Come home with your imagination.
Come home with your phone.
Come home with your affection.
Come home with your repentance.
Come home with your tenderness.
And above everything else—
come home to Christ.
Because your spouse cannot be your Savior.
A wonderful marriage cannot wash away your sin.
Sexual fulfillment cannot heal the deepest hunger of the human soul.
Only Jesus can reconcile sinners to God.
And perhaps this is where somebody finally realizes that the real emptiness was never merely sexual.
You kept asking bodies to satisfy a thirst they were never created to satisfy.
You wanted another image.
Another fantasy.
Another person.
Another experience.
Another secret.
Another rush.
But underneath all of it was a soul starving for God.
Jesus does not offer another temporary intoxication.
He offers Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
A new heart.
A new direction.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return here:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
You may need these words again when temptation whispers that covenant is boring and forbidden things are exciting.
Not for empty numbers.
Send it privately to someone fighting pornography.
Send it to the believer drowning in sexual shame.
Send it to the person who needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ has not stopped calling sinners home.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the curious.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but cannot stop wondering whether Jesus might actually be who Christians say He is.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
Christian generosity is not spiritual extortion.
“God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your support can help Gospel Warrior keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building the free library.
Keep putting Christ-centered resources into the hands of people who may never be able to pay for them.
Keep carrying the message farther.
God cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But Gospel work can still be generously supported by people who believe in helping it reach others.
That costs nothing.
Yet somewhere in your network may be a husband staring at temptation tonight.
A wife wondering whether she is still beautiful.
A marriage quietly bleeding.
A believer drowning in pornography.
A wounded spouse blaming herself for somebody else’s betrayal.
A Christian carrying sexual shame from years ago.
A sinner convinced Jesus could never want him back.
You do not know whose screen this will reach because you pressed “Share.”
So share it.
But whatever else you do after reading this, do not miss the point of Proverbs 5.
The world will teach you to keep looking.
God’s wisdom teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world will train you to compare.
Wisdom teaches you to cherish.
Sin whispers that forbidden water will satisfy you.
Then leaves you thirstier than before.
Jesus calls sinners out of hiding.
Back into truth.
Back into repentance.
Back into grace.
Back into the light.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Sin keeps asking you to trade what is sacred for what is exciting; grace teaches your heart to see the sacred as beautiful again.
